front.title: AI Safety and AI Governance for Social Media Algorithms During Elections: Protected Algorithm Verification and Controlled Output Finality, with a Detailed Account of Thirteen Embodiments

abstract.t:
Computation is not authority to make an output effective. Social media platforms, search engines, advertising systems and recommendation engines decide what very large numbers of people see, in what order and how widely it spreads. During an election, a referendum or a declared emergency, an undisclosed or unapproved change to such an algorithm could change what voters see without any visible change in the content itself. Outside observers have no practical way to check which algorithm was actually running when a given output reached the public, and proprietary models cannot simply be opened to inspection.
This document describes a technical architecture that verifies the algorithmic process and not the opinions expressed. A protected measurement step identifies the algorithm instance that is actually running and derives a fingerprint of its active configuration. The fingerprint is compared with an approved reference that applies to the protected period. An independent validator binds the verified algorithmic state to evidence about a specific pending output and issues a signed validation receipt. A separately scoped, non-bearer authorization may then allow an enforcement point to release the output. Before release, the enforcement point independently reconstructs the actual pending operation and checks the receipt, the authorization and its own protected state. If the running algorithm differs from the approved one, the output is withheld or routed through an explicitly authorized fallback.
The document describes thirteen embodiments in detail: separation of organic speech from algorithmic amplification, dynamic extraction of the algorithm fingerprint, approved reference registers, server and edge enforcement, transitions into and out of election and emergency periods, correspondence between execution and output, coverage of alternative delivery routes, distributed execution reconstruction, device-side display enforcement, degraded-mode recovery, continuous drift detection, confidential verification, and atomic consumption of authorization. For each embodiment it states what the embodiment teaches, how it works, where its enforcement point sits, how it fails, and what it does not claim. A cross-reference table connects each embodiment to a public Zenodo record that summarizes the same disclosure.
This document is an individual, informational technical proposal. It makes no allegation about any platform, party or election, it is not a legal opinion or a certification, and it does not claim that any law requires this architecture.
